The company was founded in 2002 by Dr. Bart Ripperger, DPM, a foot and ankle surgeon who operates three practices in Arizona. He created DOX EMR after \"wrestling with the growing administrative problems and rising costs of private practice for almost a decade.\" The company operates under two related brands: **DOX** is the EMR product, and **Starwriter** is a medical data collection component. The company tagline on its website is \"DOX EMR / Starwriter Medical Data Collection.\"\n\nDr. Ripperger also runs a separate venture, Starwriter Research Solutions (drbartssolutions.com), which leverages the structured clinical data collected through the DOX EMR for health economics and outcomes research (HEOR), real-world evidence (RWE), and decentralized clinical trials. This dual-purpose model — EMR for clinical use plus structured data collection for research — is a distinctive aspect of the company.\n\nDOX EMR is a very small company. It is not listed among major podiatry EMR market players in industry reports (which name AdvancedMD, DrChrono, athenahealth, Kareo, Compulink, etc.). It is marketed as requiring \"no templates to build and no customization required — ready to use day one,\" featuring a pre-built podiatry-specific medical database that covers \"all location, diagnosis, treatment, and plan options for conditions below the knee.\" The certified product (version 5.2, certified 2022-01-31) is a single integrated platform combining EMR, practice management, and billing — not a modular system with separately sold components.\n\nThe SED (Safety-Enhanced Design) intended user description is \"Physician and Podiatrist,\" confirming this is a physician-facing ambulatory EMR for podiatric medicine.\n\nThe product has a broad ONC certification covering clinical documentation (a)(1)-(a)(5), (a)(12), (a)(14); transitions of care (b)(1); clinical quality measures (c)(1)-(c)(3); FHIR API access (g)(7)-(g)(10); direct messaging (h)(1); and the EHI export requirement (b)(10). This indicates a full-featured clinical system, not just a limited documentation tool.\n\n### Users & Market\n\nThe primary users are podiatrists and their office staff. The system is described as suitable for podiatry practices \"of all sizes, from small clinics to enterprise-level organizations\" in settings including \"hospitals, clinics, emergency centers, surgical centers, and nursing homes\" (per SoftwareFinder). In practice, given the company's small size, it likely serves mainly small to mid-size ambulatory podiatry practices.\n\nNo specific customer counts, notable deployments, or case studies are publicly available. The company does not appear in major market share analyses of podiatry EMR software.\n\n### Modules & Functionality\n\nBased on the vendor website and third-party review sites, DOX EMR includes the following integrated modules and capabilities:\n\n**Front Office / Scheduling**\n- Appointment scheduling with a visual interface\n- Automated appointment reminders to reduce no-shows\n- Patient demographics and insurance management\n- Overbooking prevention\n\n**EMR / Clinical Documentation**\n- Podiatry-specific medical database with pre-built content for diagnoses, treatments, and plans for conditions below the knee\n- Patient charting with customizable templates aligned to podiatric needs\n- Patient assessments, diagnoses, and treatment plans\n- Medical history display (histories, medications, allergies displayed in \"DOX PA\")\n- Patient dictation capability for clinical notes\n- Graphical user interface for clinical documentation\n- Real-time data capture\n\n**E-Prescribing / Orders**\n- Autogenerated orders and prescriptions from clinical documentation\n- Ability to request diagnostic tests, procedures, and referrals directly through the system\n- The (a)(4) certification for drug-drug/drug-allergy interaction checking confirms e-prescribing capability\n\n**Patient Portal**\n- Online patient portal where patients can:\n  - Complete medical histories online (which then appear in the EMR)\n  - Access their medical history\n  - View upcoming appointments\n  - View treatment plans\n  - Access lab results\n- The (e)(1) criterion is NOT in their certification, which is unusual — but the vendor materials consistently describe a patient portal\n\n**Billing & Revenue Cycle Management**\n- Integrated medical billing\n- Automatic extraction of CPT and ICD billing codes from patient medical records\n- Invoice creation and payment monitoring\n- Insurance claim management (electronic claims submission)\n- Revenue cycle management\n- HL7 integration with external billing services (CoveMD mentioned as an example)\n- Real-time data capture linked to billing\n\n**Clinical Quality Measures**\n- Meaningful Use / MIPS attestation support\n- Clinical quality measure calculation and reporting (certified for (c)(1)-(c)(3))\n\n**Interoperability**\n- FHIR API access (certified for (g)(7)-(g)(10))\n- Direct messaging (certified for (h)(1))\n- Transitions of care / care summaries (certified for (b)(1))\n\n**Platform**\n- Cloud-based / web-based\n- Multi-platform: Windows, Mac, iOS, Android\n- Mobile access for viewing patient records remotely\n\n### Data & Content\n\nBased on the features described across vendor materials and review sites, DOX EMR stores:\n\n- **Patient demographics and insurance information** — managed in the front office module\n- Use/MIPS reporting\n- **Care summaries / transition of care documents** — per (b)(1) certification\n\n**What's unclear or not mentioned:**\n- **Imaging/radiology data**: While \"x-ray\" is mentioned Not a C-CDA section.\n- **Podiatry-specific clinical data** — the product's core value is its pre-built podiatry database covering \"all location, diagnosis, treatment, and plan options for conditions below the knee.\" This specialty-specific structured data likely exceeds what maps to standard C-CDA problem/procedure sections.\n- **Clinical quality measure data** — MIPS reporting numerators, denominators, and calculated measures. Not in C-CDA.\n- **Patient portal activity** — patient-completed medical histories, portal access logs.\n- **Orders and referrals** — while some order data may appear in C-CDA, the full order lifecycle (referral tracking, lab orders, procedure requests) likely isn't captured.\n- **Audit logs** — system access and activity records.\n- **Research data** — the Starwriter component collects structured research data; this would not be in a C-CDA export.\n\n**Assessment**: By equating their (b)(10) EHI export with a C-CDA/USCDI v1 document, DOX EMR is effectively providing only the clinical data subset that overlaps with the (g)(10) requirement. This is a textbook case of the (b)(10)/(g)(10) confusion described in EHI export assessments. A C-CDA USCDI v1 document covers roughly the same data as their FHIR US Core API — meaning the \"EHI export\" likely exports no more data than their standardized API already provides. The entire point of (b)(10) is to export *everything* the system stores, including billing, scheduling, audit trails, and specialty-specific data that doesn't fit into standard clinical document formats.\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\n- **Format**: C-CDA XML (Consolidated Clinical Document Architecture)\n- **Standard version**: USCDI v1 (the page says \"V1 standard for connection\")\n- **FHIR involvement**: None — the b(10) export is C-CDA, separate from their Aidbox FHIR API\n- **Appropriateness**: C-CDA is a recognized healthcare standard, but it is not appropriate as a *complete* EHI export format. C-CDA is designed for clinical document exchange (care summaries, referrals), not for bulk data export of an entire EHR database. It has no sections for billing data, scheduling, audit logs, or custom/specialty-specific data structures. Using C-CDA for (b)(10) means the export is structurally limited to the clinical data domains that C-CDA supports.\n- **Reconstruct-ability**: A third party could understand the clinical portions of the export by referencing the C-CDA standard, but would have no visibility into billing, scheduling, or specialty-specific podiatry data that the system stores.\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\nThe documentation is among the most minimal possible while still technically existing:\n- **One paragraph** of text describing the export format\n- **No data dictionary** at any level of granularity\n- **No field-level definitions** — not even a list of which C-CDA sections are populated\n- **No sample data** or examples\n- **No user instructions** for how to trigger the export\n- **No schema or template documentation** — the only reference is to the generic HL7 C-CDA standard, not any vendor-specific customization\n- **Not developer-implementable** — a developer could not implement an import of this data based on this documentation alone; they would need the generic C-CDA spec and would have to reverse-engineer the vendor's mapping\n\nA developer receiving a DOX EMR C-CDA export would have to rely entirely on the generic C-CDA specification to parse it, with no guidance on which sections are populated, what data elements are included, or how DOX EMR's internal data model maps to C-CDA structures.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\n- **Granularity**: Zero. Not in C-CDA.\n- **Patient portal activity** — patient-completed medical histories, portal access logs.\n- **Orders and referrals** — while some order data may appear in C-CDA, the full order lifecycle (referral tracking, lab orders, procedure requests) likely isn't captured.\n- **Audit logs** — system access and activity records.\n- **Research data** — the Starwriter component collects structured research data; this would not be in a C-CDA export.\n\n**Assessment**: By equating their (b)(10) EHI export with a C-CDA/USCDI v1 document, DOX EMR is effectively providing only the clinical data subset that overlaps with the (g)(10) requirement. A C-CDA USCDI v1 document covers roughly the same data as their FHIR US Core API — meaning the \"EHI export\" likely exports no more data than their standardized API already provides. The entire point of (b)(10) is to export *everything* the system stores, including billing, scheduling, audit trails, and specialty-specific data that doesn't fit into standard clinical document formats.\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\n- **Format**: C-CDA XML (Consolidated Clinical Document Architecture)\n- **Standard version**: USCDI v1 (the page says \"V1 standard for connection\")\n- **FHIR involvement**: None — the b(10) export is C-CDA, separate from their Aidbox FHIR API\n- **Appropriateness**: C-CDA is a recognized healthcare standard, but it is not appropriate as a *complete* EHI export format. C-CDA is designed for clinical document exchange (care summaries, referrals), not for bulk data export of an entire EHR database. It has no sections for billing data, scheduling, audit logs, or custom/specialty-specific data structures. Using C-CDA for (b)(10) means the export is structurally limited to the clinical data domains that C-CDA supports.\n- **Reconstruct-ability**: A third party could understand the clinical portions of the export by referencing the C-CDA standard, but would have no visibility into billing, scheduling, or specialty-specific podiatry data that the system stores.\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\nThe documentation is among the most minimal possible while still technically existing:\n- **One paragraph** of text describing the export format\n- **No data dictionary** at any level of granularity\n- **No field-level definitions** — not even a list of which C-CDA sections are populated\n- **No sample data** or examples\n- **No user instructions** for how to trigger the export\n- **No schema or template documentation** — the only reference is to the generic HL7 C-CDA standard, not any vendor-specific customization\n- **Not developer-implementable** — a developer could not implement an import of this data based on this documentation alone; they would need the generic C-CDA spec and would have to reverse-engineer the vendor's mapping\n\nA developer receiving a DOX EMR C-CDA export would have to rely entirely on the generic C-CDA specification to parse it, with no guidance on which sections are populated, what data elements are included, or how DOX EMR's internal data model maps to C-CDA structures.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\n- **Granularity**: Zero.
